findings.summary: Fan-out cost figure is stated with an unexplained assumption that differs from the 'avg' used elsewhere, mixing average follower count into a line that reads as exact.
findings.fix: Label '200 = average followers per account' so it is not read as a fixed per-user figure.

findings.summary: Page 3 states the PUBLISHED state is reached after transcode, but the post-state diagram shows UPLOADING before POST /v1/posts even though media upload happens before the post call, so post state and media state are conflated.
findings.fix: Label these as post states beginning at PROCESSING (created on POST), and keep UPLOADING as a media state only, as on page 9 (PROCESSING, READY, FAILED).

findings.summary: The follow flow says the follower's feed is a Redis list, but elsewhere the feed is a Redis ZSET.
The Follow Graph page states the follow flow backfills 'Redis list' while page 7 defines the feed as a Redis ZSET, so the same thing is named inconsistently.
findings.fix: Say 'feed ZSET updated' to match pages 7, 10 and 12.

findings.summary: Page 5 and page 6 call the cached feed a 'feed list' while page 7 defines it as a sorted set, so the term varies for the same thing.
findings.evidence: Feed list lives in the Redis feed cache; "each follower's feed list"
findings.fix: Use 'feed ZSET' (or 'feed cache entry') consistently across pages.

findings.summary: The pull cost line mixes peak read QPS with a merge across 200 timelines, which asserts a scale not reconciled with the feed cache hit assumptions and is a long compound bullet.
findings.evidence: Pull: ~200 timelines merged per open, at 170K QPS peak
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: timelines merged per open, then peak fetches/s.

findings.summary: The per-user feed memory estimate treats each ZSET member as 8 bytes, but Redis stores members as strings and adds per-entry skiplist and hash overhead.
findings.evidence: Member = post_id (8 bytes) ... 800 post_ids x 8 B | ~6.4 KB ... 500M x 6.4 KB | ~3.2 TB
findings.fix: Say the raw payload is 8 B per id and that real Redis ZSET memory is roughly 50-100+ B per entry. That makes about 40-80 KB per user and 20-40 TB in total. Alternatively, present 3.2 TB explicitly as a lower bound.

findings.summary: The hot-counter example uses MGET on 16 keys spread across shards, which fails with CROSSSLOT in Redis Cluster unless the keys share a hash tag. A shared hash tag would put them all on one shard and defeat the point of splitting.
findings.evidence: MGET likes:9001:0 likes:9001:1 ... likes:9001:15 ... Writes spread over 16 keys; the sum is the count
findings.fix: Read the 16 sub-counters with parallel per-key GETs or a pipeline, or note that MGET only works if the keys sit in the same slot. Do not claim MGET gives a cross-shard sum.

findings.summary: The cursor query is shown twice with different forms on pages 7, 10, 11 and 12 (ZREVRANGE by rank on page 7, inclusive score on page 10, exclusive '(' on page 12, LIMIT 0 40 on page 11), so the pagination rule is stated inconsistently.
findings.evidence: ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:42 1730100000123 -inf ... "Inclusive score; drop ids at that score already seen" vs "ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:42 (1730000000000 -inf LIMIT 0 20"
findings.fix: Pick one form (inclusive score plus dropping seen ids) and use it on pages 10, 11 and 12.

findings.summary: Code blocks for pagination and counters appear while the idea is stated only partly beforehand, and the like flow packs several ideas into one bullet.
findings.evidence: Peak ~100K like events/s: Redis INCR absorbs them, the DB gets batched writes
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: INCR absorbs peak, DB gets batched writes.

findings.summary: The text says a lost Redis shard falls back to a cached stale feed. Page 7 says the shard's feeds vanish, so there is no cached copy to serve.
findings.evidence: Redis shard lost: serve a cached stale feed, rebuild lazily by pull
findings.fix: Say: serve from a replica if one exists, otherwise rebuild by pull on the next open. Or fall back to chronological pull for that user.

findings.summary: The cheatsheet cursor query uses an exclusive score bound, which contradicts the page 10 and 11 rule for same-millisecond ties.
findings.evidence: ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:42 (1730000000000 -inf LIMIT 0 20 … cursor = (score, post_id); drop already-seen ids
findings.fix: Use the inclusive form `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:42 1730000000000 -inf LIMIT 0 20`, as on page 10. Keep the note to drop already-seen ids at that score, so posts tied on the same millisecond are not skipped.

findings.summary: The sub-counter increment rule contradicts page 10. Page 10 picks the sub-counter by user_id % 16, and page 13 picks a random one.
findings.evidence: INCR likes:9001:7   # shard = user_id % 16 (page 10) vs. "INCR a random one" (page 13)
findings.fix: Use one rule in both places. Either choose the sub-counter by hash(user_id) % 16, or say a random choice is safe because the SET NX dedupe key already prevents double counting.

findings.summary: The quiz answer picks a random sub-counter for a like, but page 10 teaches choosing it by user_id.
findings.evidence: quiz: "INCR a random one, and sum all 16 on read" vs page 10: "INCR likes:9001:7   # shard = user_id % 16"
findings.fix: Make the quiz match page 10 with "INCR sub-counter user_id % 16". Alternatively, say on page 10 that any sub-counter works for increments and that only the sum matters.

findings.summary: The quiz dedupes likes by inserting into the likes table first, but page 10 teaches a Redis SET NX dedupe key in front of INCR and Kafka.
findings.evidence: quiz: "insert into likes(post_id, user_id) with a unique key, and INCR only if the insert is new" vs page 10 flow: "SET NX dedupe key -> INCR only if new -> Kafka -> Consumer INSERT likes"
findings.fix: Align the quiz with the page 10 flow: SET NX on the dedupe key, INCR only if the key is new, then let the consumer insert into likes, where the unique key is the source of truth.

findings.summary: Check-yourself answers are long prose-style bullet lists with several ideas each, harder to skim.
findings.evidence: Many more accounts become pull-based, so each feed read must fetch and merge many more celebrity timelines
findings.fix: Shorten each answer to a single cause bullet and a single fix bullet.
